_doc.purpose: Default-deny allowlist of OpenRouter provider slugs. The user's rule, first written 2026-09-06 as 'my data never routes to China' and restated 2026-09-20 as what it always meant: a request may only be SERVED in the United States, Canada or Europe. The model's nationality was never the question -- Chinese models (GLM, and Qwen/DeepSeek/Kimi behind it) are wanted, and wanted on hardware outside China -- because on OpenRouter the model alone decides nothing, the serving PROVIDER does. So the provider set is pinned here and enforced by scripts/container/openrouter-guard.py -- not by any client setting a client could change.
_doc.enforced_by: scripts/container/openrouter-guard.py rewrites every completion request body's `provider` object before forwarding it to openrouter.ai. Clients never hold the real key; they hold a guard token and the guard's loopback base URL.

openrouter_fields.provider.only: string[] -- the ONLY providers allowed for the request. The guard sets this to [.allow[].slug] on every completion request, which is what makes the allowlist default-deny.
openrouter_fields.provider.allow_fallbacks: boolean, OpenRouter default true -- whether a backup provider may serve the request. Forced to false (.force.allow_fallbacks) so a failed allowlisted provider is an error, never a silent hop somewhere else.
openrouter_fields.provider.data_collection: "allow" | "deny", OpenRouter default "allow" -- forced to "deny" (.force.data_collection) so providers that may store prompts are skipped.
openrouter_fields.provider.order: string[] -- providers to try in order. A client-supplied order is KEPT only when every entry is in .allow; otherwise (missing, empty, or naming a provider outside .allow) it is dropped and logged, and the guard forces this policy's own .order instead -- an empty order left OpenRouter free to try only its default pick inside .only, which stayed 429 for 15+ minutes on 2026-09-17 (claude-orca-c6b) while a named fallback provider answered at once.
openrouter_fields.provider.ignore: string[] -- providers to skip. Not used: with provider.only set to the allowlist, everything else is already excluded. .deny below is documentation of WHY a host is out, and the source for the guard's log and the docs.

_doc.slug_source: Slugs are the `tag` prefix before '/' in https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/models/<author>/<slug>/endpoints, cross-checked against https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/providers (slug + headquarters + datacenters), verified 2026-09-06 and re-read 2026-09-20. `lambda` and `hyperbolic` were on the user's candidate list but no longer exist in the OpenRouter provider registry, so they are not listed; a slug that is not in the registry can never be selected anyway.
_doc.country: The country a request's prompt is processed in, as far as it can be established from the provider's headquarters and declared datacenters. A provider with no establishable country is NOT allowed -- absence of evidence is denial here.
_doc.allowed_countries: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 codes a request may be served in: US, CA, and Europe (EU-27 + EEA + CH + GB). This is the rule itself, in machine-readable form: the guard refuses to start if any .allow entry names a country outside this set, so a provider row can no longer quietly widen the residency boundary -- widening it takes an edit to THIS list, which is the edit a human reviews. It also means a new host is admitted by the rule rather than by a fresh judgement call: a Canadian provider (the registry lists none today) or another European one is allowed as soon as its country is established, on the same evidence the rest of .allow rests on. Countries absent from the list -- China first among them, but equally SG, IL, ID, and 'unverified' -- are denied by the same line.

allow.name: DigitalOcean
allow.note: US company (New York); the OpenRouter registry leaves its headquarters field blank.

allow.name: Inceptron
allow.note: Swedish company, Finnish datacenter -- headquarters AND a declared datacenter both inside the allowed set, which is stronger evidence than several older entries here carry. Denied until 2026-09-20 for being off the user's hand-written candidate list; the country rule, not a list, is what admits it now. Serves GLM 5.3.

allow.name: NextBit
allow.note: Spanish company, Spanish datacenter (registry, 2026-09-20). Never denied, just never listed -- default-deny meant absent. Serves GLM 5.3 flash.

deny.name: Z.AI
deny.reason: Zhipu AI, Beijing; the OpenRouter registry lists a Singapore entity, which does not change who operates it. Serves GLM first-party -- the model is wanted, this host is not.

deny.reason: China-based host.

deny.name: Novita
deny.reason: Registry self-reports a US headquarters but declares no datacenter; GPU capacity is resold across regions and the serving location cannot be verified. Denied by default (user list, 2026-09-06).

deny.reason: US company, but Workers AI runs on an anycast edge network with datacenters in mainland China among 300+ locations, and the registry declares none of them. A request's serving city is not knowable in advance. Denied by default (2026-09-20).
